1:1.t: Philippi: see Acts 16:12-40, where the church began. "Overseers": the KJV's "bishops"; see Acts 20:28.

1:13.t: "The whole palace guard": the KJV's "all the palace"; Greek praitorion, the imperial guard, or the governor's headquarters if Paul wrote from Caesarea or Ephesus.

1:16.t: The KJV gives these verses in this order; many early manuscripts reverse them.

2:17.t: A drink offering of wine was poured out on or beside a sacrifice (Numbers 15:1-10). Paul pictures his possible death this way.

3:2.t: "Mutilators of the flesh": the KJV's "the concision", a wordplay on "circumcision" (Greek katatome, peritome). Paul means those who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised.

3:3.t: "By His Spirit": the KJV's "in the spirit"; many early manuscripts read "by the Spirit of God".

3:8.t: "Garbage": the KJV's "dung"; Greek skybala, refuse or excrement.

3:16.t: "Walking by the same rule and keeping the same mind": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

4:2.t: Euodia and Syntyche were women who had worked with Paul.

4:3.t: "True companion": the KJV's "true yokefellow"; Greek syzygos, which may also be a personal name, Syzygus.

4:13.t: "Through Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "through Him".
"I can do all things": in context, Paul means bearing every circumstance, plenty or want, through Christ's strength.

4:22.t: "Caesar's household": servants and officials of the emperor, not necessarily his family.

1:5.t: "Partnership" (Greek koinonia): see Acts 2:42. The Philippians shared in Paul's work through prayer and gifts (4:15).

1:21.t: "To live is Christ and to die is gain": Christ is the whole of Paul's life, and death will bring him into Christ's presence (1:23).

2:6.t: Many think these verses were an early Christian hymn. "In very nature God" (Greek en morphe theou): the KJV's "in the form of God"; morphe means the essential form, not mere appearance. "Something to be grasped" (Greek harpagmos): the KJV's "robbery"; something to be seized or clung to for His own advantage. "Made Himself nothing" (Greek heauton ekenosen): the KJV's "made himself of no reputation", literally "emptied Himself". He did not stop being God; He set aside His rights and glory, taking the nature of a servant. Christians have long debated the exact sense of this "self-emptying" (kenosis).

2:10.t: Echoing Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to the LORD. Paul applies the words to Jesus. "Lord" (Greek kyrios): see Romans 10:9.

2:12.t: "Work out your salvation ... it is God who works in you": not earning salvation but living it out, because God is at work within. Both sides are held together.

3:9.t: "Faith in Christ": see Romans 3:22. "Righteousness ... from God": see Romans 1:17.

3:10.t: "Know" (Greek gnonai): to know personally. See Matthew 7:23. "Participation" (Greek koinonia): the KJV's "fellowship". See Acts 2:42.

3:20.t: "Citizenship" (Greek politeuma): the KJV's "conversation", which in 1611 meant way of life. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were citizens of Rome; believers are citizens of heaven.

4:5.t: "Gentleness" (Greek epieikes): the KJV's "moderation", reasonableness, a yielding, gracious spirit.

4:6.t: "Do not be anxious" (Greek merimnate): the KJV's "Be careful for nothing", "careful" meaning "full of care". See Matthew 6:25.

4:7.t: "Guard" (Greek phrouresei): the KJV's "keep", a military word: God's peace stands sentry over the heart.

4:11.t: "Content" (Greek autarkes): self-sufficient. The Stoics used it of independence from circumstances; Paul's contentment rests on Christ (4:13). "Learned the secret" (Greek memyemai): to be initiated, a term from the mystery religions.
